knowledge_point.title: Differentiating a Quotient Containing Other Functions

question.:question/problem:
If a curve $C$ is given by $y=\frac{2 \cos{\left(x \right)}}{\sin{\left(x \right)} + 1}$, calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=\frac{\pi}{2}.$

The slope is {{field-1}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
In this case, the expression for $y$ is a quotient $\frac{u(x)}{v(x)}$ with $u(x)=2 \cos{\left(x \right)}$ and $v(x)=\sin{\left(x \right)} + 1.$

Therefore, we apply the quotient rule as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f^{\prime}(x)&=\frac{u^{\prime}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot v^{\prime}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}}\\ &=\frac{(2 \cos{\left(x \right)})^{\prime}\cdot (\sin{\left(x \right)} + 1)-(2 \cos{\left(x \right)})\cdot (\sin{\left(x \right)} + 1)^{\prime}}{(\sin{\left(x \right)} + 1)^{2}}\\ &=\frac{(- 2 \sin{\left(x \right)})\cdot (\sin{\left(x \right)} + 1)-(2 \cos{\left(x \right)})\cdot (\cos{\left(x \right)})}{(\sin{\left(x \right)} + 1)^{2}}\\ &=\frac{- 2 \sin^{2}{\left(x \right)} - 2 \sin{\left(x \right)} - 2 \cos^{2}{\left(x \right)}}{\left(\sin{\left(x \right)} + 1\right)^{2}}\\ &=\frac{-2\sin x-2(\sin^2 x+\cos^2 x)}{\left(\sin{\left(x \right)} + 1\right)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\sin^2 x+\cos^2 x=1$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f^{\prime}(x)&=\frac{- 2 \sin{\left(x \right)} - 2}{\left(\sin{\left(x \right)} + 1\right)^{2}}\\ &=\frac{-2(1+\sin x)}{\left(\sin{\left(x \right)} + 1\right)^{2}}\\ &=\frac{-2}{1+\sin x}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}f^{\prime}(\frac{\pi}{2})&=\frac{-2}{1+\sin (\frac{\pi}{2})}\\ &=\frac{-2}{2}\\ &=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $-1.$
